title: The Lotus Opens at Midnight
summary: At midnight a lotus opens full and thirty-two yoginīs thrill. The moon, set moving along the path of the avadhūtī, goes into nirvāṇa while a lotus plant carries the lotus along a conduit, and Bhusuku says that in union he has understood innate joy, great bliss, in play. Munidatta reads the hour as that of the wisdom-knowledge empowerment, the lotus as the practitioner's uṣṇīṣa lotus and the yoginīs as the thirty-two channels that carry bodhicitta (cp.27.m2); for him the moon is bodhicitta reaching the vajra peak, and the lotus plant is the purified avadhūtikā, Nairātmā (cp.27.m3, cp.27.m4).

flags.note: The poet's name comes from the attribution bhusukupādānām ("of Bhusukupāda"), which Shastri prints before the song; the edited text has removed it from the head of 1a. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names the poet 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs and the melody 'dod pa sbyin pa (see notes).

bhara: I read it as "full", describing the opening lotus, as the Tibetan line does (chu skyes khengs rgyas, "the lotus filled and opened"). It could instead go with adharāti as a postposition, "all through midnight" or "at the height of midnight" (compare Hindi rāt bhar, "all night long"). Munidatta does not gloss it (cp.27.m2).
bikasau: I read it as a past participle, "opened", with Munidatta's vikasitaṃ (cp.27.m2). A present tense, "opens", is possible.

The Tibetan moves "thirty-two" (sum cu gnyis), the first word of 1b, to the end of this line, apparently to fill its nine-syllable metre. Read that way, the number could belong to the lotus (or lotuses). Munidatta's comment, in both versions, gives the number to the yoginīs (cp.27.m2).

lines.translit: batisa joiṇī tasu aṅga uhnasiu || dhru ||
lines.gloss: thirty-two · yoginī(s) · its (his, her) · limb(s), body · thrilled · refrain cue (not translated)

flags.note: tasu aṅga, "its (his, her) limbs": tasu is a singular genitive. The limbs may belong to the lotus (my "its"; the yoginīs would then be in apposition, perhaps its parts), to the yoginīs (if tasu stands loosely for a plural, giving "their limbs thrilled"), or to an unnamed person. Munidatta says the thrill of the limbs arose from "their" joys, the yoginīs', without saying whose limbs (cp.27.m2). The Tibetan line has de la, "in that" or "to that". The comma keeps the source's asyndeton rather than choosing.

uhnasiu is perhaps a misreading of uhlasiu (Sanskrit ullasita, "thrilled, gladdened"), since হ্ন and হ্ল are close in form. Munidatta's aṅgohnāsa (cp.27.m2) has the same spelling. The Tibetan has tshim, "sated, satisfied". "Thrilled" follows the ullasita reading.
Shastri prints ধ্রু after this couplet too, though couplet 2 is the refrain: Munidatta comments on couplet 2 "with the refrain" (dhruvapadena, cp.27.m3). Not translated.

lines.gloss: set moving · moon ("hare-bearer") · on the path · avadhūtī
lines.en: The [moon]{moon} was set moving along the [path]{marga} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti};

flags.note: cāliua: I take it as a passive participle, "set moving", as Munidatta's pracalita (cp.27.m4) and the Tibetan bskyod take it. It could be an absolutive, "having set the moon moving", with the subject of 2b as the one who sets it moving. It differs from cālia in 3a by an extra u, which may be a misprint.
māge abadhūi: "on the path, the avadhūtī" or "on the avadhūtī's path". The genitive follows Munidatta's avadhūtīmārgeṇa (cp.27.m3); the Tibetan has lam a wa d+hU tIr, "the path, into the avadhūtī".

lines.gloss: from / by the jewel · the innate (locative, or nominative in -e) · tells · refrain cue (not translated)
lines.en: through the [jewel]{ratna} it tells of the [innate]{sahaja}.

flags.note: Who tells? raaṇahu is most likely ablative or instrumental ("from" or "by the jewel"), and kahei is a third-person present. I take the moon of 2a as the subject, as Munidatta (sa ... kathayati, cp.27.m3) and the Tibetan comment do. ṣahaje could instead be an eastern nominative in -e, giving "from the jewel the innate speaks", or the subject could be an unnamed "he".
The Tibetan line has "the precious word speaks the innate" (rin chen tshig ni lhan cig skyes pa smra). It supplies "word", which the Bengali lacks, and makes it the subject (see notes).

lines.gloss: set moving · moon ("hare-bearer") · went · into nirvāṇa

flags.note: gau, "went" (Sanskrit gata), is past; the Tibetan line has the present 'gro, "goes".

lines.gloss: lotus plant · lotus · carries / flows · by the conduit · refrain cue (not translated)
lines.en: the [lotus plant]{kamalini} carries the [lotus]{lotus} along the [conduit]{pranala}.

flags.note: kamalini can be a lotus plant or a bed or pond of lotuses, and bahai can mean "carries" or "flows". "Carries" follows Munidatta's transitive vahati (cp.27.m4). The Tibetan line takes the verb as "flowing" and the lotus as the goal (see notes).

lines.gloss: joy of cessation · vilakṣaṇa ("beyond characteristics") · pure

flags.note: Shastri prints ॥, which normally closes a couplet, after 4a. But the sense runs on: 4a names what 4b says is understood. As instructed, 4a and 4b are treated as one couplet, and the colon carries the run-on.

bilakṣaṇa sudha: I read the two words as one phrase, "purified by vilakṣaṇa", as Munidatta takes them (vilakṣaṇacaturthānandaśuddha, "purified by vilakṣaṇa, the fourth joy", cp.27.m5). They could also be three separate items ("the joy of cessation, vilakṣaṇa, the pure"). bilakṣaṇa can also be the ordinary adjective "extraordinary". The Tibetan line has "the joy of cessation, free of characteristics" and nothing for "pure".

lines.translit: jo ethu bujhai so ethu budha || dhru ||
lines.gloss: who(ever) · here · understands · he · here · wise / buddha · refrain cue (not translated)
lines.en: whoever understands it here is a [buddha]{buddha} here.

flags.note: budha: I render it "a buddha", spelled budha as often, following the Tibetan sangs rgyas and Munidatta, who calls the one who understands the Blessed Vajradhara (cp.27.m5). It is also Sanskrit budha, "wise", which would give "is wise here" and a play on bujhai, "understands".
ethu, "here" (Apabhraṃśa etthu), occurs twice, and I keep both. "It" is supplied for what 4a names. The Tibetan takes the first ethu as "that" (de), the object of knowing, and leaves out the second.

lines.gloss: Bhusuku · says · I (by me) · understood · in union

flags.note: melem̐: I read it as a locative, "in union", as Munidatta does ("in the union of wisdom and means", prajñopāyamelake, cp.27.m6). The Tibetan line makes it the object of knowing, "I knew the gathering" (see notes).
I use the glossary's English for p-bhusuku, "Bhusukupāda", although the poet calls himself simply Bhusuku. See questions.

lines.gloss: innate joy · great bliss · in play · refrain cue (not translated)

flags.note: lolem̐: I render it "in play", taking it as a form of līlā, with Munidatta's līlayā (cp.27.m6) and the Tibetan rol. Sanskrit lola, "swaying, eager", is a less likely source. The Tibetan line makes rol the main verb: "revels in innate joy, great bliss".

notes.text: rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each song's heading names the rāga it is sung to, here Kāmoda. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) calls the melody 'dod pa sbyin pa, "giving what is desired", as if the name were Sanskrit kāmada.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) attributes the song to 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs, "the one of the three notions", which the glossary records as a Tibetan name for Bhusuku. It probably reflects the traditional explanation of the name as three syllables standing for three activities (eating, sleeping and going about, in the usual telling). I have not checked that explanation against a source here.
Munidatta introduces the song as the siddha master Bhusuku, "full of the juice of innate joy", setting out "that same meaning" (cp.27.m1), presumably the subject of the song before it.

The image is a lotus opening full at midnight and thirty-two yoginīs, women adepts, thrilled. In Indian poetic convention the day lotus (kamala) opens to the sun and closes at night, while water lilies open under the moon. A kamala opening at midnight may therefore be one of the songs' deliberate reversals. Munidatta supplies a sun: the lotus is opened "by the ray of the vajra-sun" (cp.27.m2).

Munidatta sets the scene at midnight, "at the fourth juncture", when the wisdom-knowledge empowerment is conferred according to the rite of "the chapter on empowerment" (sekapaṭala). He calls the lotus "my uṣṇīṣa lotus", the lotus at the crown of the head (cp.27.m2). The Tibetan comment's nam phyed kyi thun mtshams bzhi can also be read "the four junctures of midnight".

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads nam phyed chu skyes khengs rgyas sum cu gnyis: "at midnight the lotus filled and opened, thirty-two". It takes bhara as khengs, "filled, full", which supports "opened full". It also ends the line with "thirty-two", which the Bengali has at the start of 1b. This is probably to make up its nine-syllable line, but it leaves open whether the number counts the lotus or lotuses or the yoginīs.

Munidatta reads "thirty-two yoginīs" as the thirty-two channels that carry bodhicitta. He names lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtī, and adds "Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā and the rest". These, he says, flow into that place, and the mass of their joys, beginning with joy, made the limbs thrill (cp.27.m2). Abhedyā ("indivisible") and Sūkṣmarūpā ("of subtle form") look like the first two names in the Hevajra Tantra's list of thirty-two channels. That should be checked before the commentary is woven.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rnal 'byor ma rnams de la yan lag tshim: "the yoginīs, in that, limbs satisfied". It has tshim, "sated, satisfied", for uhnasiu, and de la, "in" or "to that", which may answer to tasu; it leaves open whose limbs are meant, as the Bengali does.

ṣaṣahara is Sanskrit śaśadhara or śaśahara, "the hare-bearer", a stock name for the moon, whose markings Indian tradition sees as a hare. The Tibetan keeps the figure (ri bong 'dzin, "hare-holder"). It is rendered "moon", as in the glossary. avadhūtī (the song's abadhūi), literally "she who has shaken off", is the name tantric yoga gives to the central channel of the subtle body. The song itself names it here, so it stays in the line in source form.

Munidatta says the refrain states the power of the true guru. At that time the hare-bearer, the moon of bodhicitta, went by the path of the avadhūtī to the vajra peak. By the power of "the jewel of reality that is the true guru's word", it tells innate joy "in me" (cp.27.m3). Where the Sanskrit has "in me" (mayi), the Tibetan comment has "to them" (de dag la).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rin chen tshig ni lhan cig skyes pa smra: "the precious word speaks the innate". The word "word" (tshig) has no counterpart in the Bengali. It makes the jewel speech and the subject of the verb, close to Munidatta's "jewel of reality that is the true guru's word" (cp.27.m3). This is a reading, so it is not followed in the line.

Munidatta's quotation from Saraha begins citte śaśaharam in Shastri, with the syllable ha restored by the editor (cp.27.m3). The Tibetan comment gives the opening as sems kyi dbang po'i mda', "the arrow of the lord of the mind". That looks like a reading of the unrestored letters as citteśa-śara, "the arrow of the mind's lord". So the Tibetan does not support the restored "moon" (śaśahara) in the quotation.

Munidatta takes the moon as bodhicitta. Set moving along the path of the avadhūtī, it went, through the guru's lineage, to nirvāṇa, which he calls clear light, at the tip of the vajra peak (cp.27.m4).
paṇāla (Sanskrit praṇāla, praṇālī) is a conduit, spout or drain for water. kamalinī, from kamala, "lotus", is a lotus plant, or a bed or pond of lotuses.

Munidatta derives kamalinī as "she who has lotus juice", the juice of great bliss. He identifies her with the naturally purified avadhūtikā, Nairātmā. With the lotus juice, which is bodhicitta, the juice of great bliss, she gladdens the body-vajra and carries it to the region of the wheel of great bliss (cp.27.m4). Whether "it" is the juice or the body-vajra, the sentence does not make clear. He takes the song's lotus as "lotus juice" and does not gloss the conduit.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads pad+ma can ni pad+mar 'bab pa'i chu: "the one with the lotus is water flowing into the lotus". It takes bahai as "flowing" rather than "carries", makes the lotus the goal rather than the thing carried, and has "flowing water" where the Bengali has paṇālem̐, "by the conduit". The syntax of the line is therefore open to doubt.

Shastri's footnote says that the passage he marks in Munidatta's comment on this couplet had been lost and was restored (cp.27.m4); I have not seen the footnote itself. I take that passage to be the stretch between his two marks (shown as ❌), from rasam asyāstīti kamalinī to tam eva bodhicittamahāsukha. Both marks follow the word mahāsukha, the pattern of an eye-skip, in which a copyist jumps from one mahāsukha to the next. The stretch contains the whole gloss of kamalinī. The Tibetan translation has the same content (pad+ma'i ro la bde ba chen po'i ro de yod pa'i phyir ro / pad+ma can ni de nyid rang bzhin yongs su dag pa a wa d+hU tI pa bdag med ma ...), so the restored words were in the text the Tibetan translators had. The Tibetan also renders the quoted line of Kṛṣṇācārya differently (rab tu 'bab pas rang sems 'ching, "flowing strongly, it binds one's own mind"), as if reading something like ṇiamaṇa, "one's own mind", for Shastri's ṇiamara.

vilakṣaṇa, "beyond characteristics", is kept in source form. In the Hevajra system it is the last of the four moments of yogic union; in ordinary Sanskrit the word also means "different, extraordinary". viramānanda, "the joy of cessation", is one of the four joys of yogic union.

Munidatta says this joy of cessation is purified by vilakṣaṇa, the fourth joy. The lord of yogis in whom understanding arose, day and night, by the guru's grace is himself the Blessed Vajradhara, with the thirty-two marks and the eighty signs. There is no room here, he adds, for those who have not understood reality (cp.27.m5). His Vajradhara supports reading budha as "a buddha". For "those who have not understood reality", the Tibetan comment has "ignorance of the realities".

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads khyad par dga' ba mtshan nyid dang bral ba ("the joy of cessation, free of characteristics") and gang gis de shes de ni sangs rgyas so ("whoever knows that, he is a buddha"). The first line has nothing for sudha, "pure", though the Tibetan comment has dag pa (cp.27.m5). The second takes budha as sangs rgyas, "buddha", and the first ethu as de, "that".

Munidatta says the last couplet makes firm the poet's own understanding. He paraphrases: "by me, Bhusukupāda, in the union of wisdom and means, innate joy, great bliss, was understood playfully (līlayā), by the true guru's grace" (cp.27.m6). The Tibetan comment ends instead "having understood it by the true guru's kindness, (I) revel" (rol pa'o), making the play a verb, as the Tibetan line does.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads b+hu su kus smras bdag gis tshogs pa shes ("Bhusuku said: I knew the gathering") and lhan cig skyes dga' bde ba chen por rol ("revel in innate joy, great bliss"). It takes melem̐ as tshogs pa, "gathering, assembly", the object of knowing, where Munidatta has "in the union" (cp.27.m6). It takes lolem̐ as the main verb, rol, "revel, play".

termsOmitted.reason: In the Tibetan line dga' ba occurs only inside khyad par dga' ba, the joy of cessation, which is marked as viramananda.

questions: The glossary's English for p-bhusuku is "Bhusukupāda", which I used in the bhaṇitā (5a) as the rules require. The poet calls himself simply Bhusuku, and the -pāda honorific is not his. Should "Bhusuku" be added as a variant for his self-naming, as "Kāṇha" is used for Kāṇha?

1b, "thirty-two yoginīs, its limbs thrilled": the singular tasu leaves open whose limbs thrill (the lotus's, the yoginīs', or an unnamed person's). Do you prefer the open "its", or "their limbs thrilled"? And do you accept "thrilled" on the conjecture uhnasiu = uhlasiu (ullasita)?
1a, bhara: "opened full" (with the Tibetan khengs) or "all through midnight" (bhara as a postposition)?

2b: I made the moon the subject of kahei ("it tells of the innate"), as Munidatta and the Tibetan comment do. Should the line stay open instead (for example "the innate speaks", taking ṣahaje as a nominative)?
4a: Is "purified by vilakṣaṇa" (Munidatta's compound reading) acceptable, or would you rather list the words ("the joy of cessation, vilakṣaṇa, pure")? The Tibetan line has no "pure".
4b: "a buddha" or "wise" for budha? And is the supplied "it" ("whoever understands it here") acceptable for the run-on from 4a?
3b: "carries" (Munidatta's vahati) or "flows" (the Tibetan 'bab pa) for bahai?

Shastri's footnote on the lost and restored passage: I worked from the description in my brief, not the footnote itself. Please confirm that the passage is the stretch of cp.27.m4 between the two marks (the kamalinī gloss), as my witness note on couplet 3 assumes.

For the weave stage: in cp.27.m2, are "Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā and the rest" names of channels from the Hevajra Tantra's list of thirty-two? And in cp.27.m3, should Shastri's restored ha in Saraha's citte śaśaharam stand, given the Tibetan "arrow of the lord of the mind"?
